articles.title: Impact of drought 'can be seen along River Severn'
articles.summary: One Worcestershire fisherman said water levels were probably the lowest he had seen.
articles.body:
The impact of this year's drought can be seen along parts of the River Severn, people who use the river have said.

Geoff Maguire from Kidderminster and District Angling Association said water levels were probably the lowest he had seen.

Natural Resources Wales has applied to the Welsh Government for a Drought Order on the river while the Environment Agency (EA) has submitted a matching application for the English stretch.

If approved, the order would temporarily reduce the minimum amount of water legally required in the river.

Currently, water is being released by reservoirs in Wales and pumped from groundwater in Shropshire to help keep the river flowing but the EA says those supplies are under increasing pressure.

Clywedog Reservoir in Powys is currently at about 48% capacity, according to the Environment Agency, and its level has been falling rapidly.

Matt Lawrence, the agency's environment programme manager, said: "We really want to protect that resource or else we potentially can see sections of the upper Severn dry up completely.

"That will have a terrible effect on wildlife, the ecology of the river and the users of the river," he added.

About 200m litres a day are also being pumped into the Severn from a groundwater scheme in Shropshire.

Lawrence said the groundwater was currently in a "good state" but needed to be closely monitored.

"We're having to go out in the river to find enough water to fish, but it's not just us - I think it's the canoes and the boats that are really struggling to get over certain areas," Maguire said.

Fishing conditions have remained good in some areas, but Maguire said anglers were increasingly concerned about what lower levels could mean.

The Severn, which at 224 miles (360km) is longest river in Great Britain, is home to a wide range of wildlife including salmon, eels, otters, brown trout and European bullhead.

Its smaller tributaries and headwaters are particularly important habitats.

Safina Akhtar-Watters, a citizen scientist and first-year environmental science student from Worcestershire, said drought could threaten these ecosystems.

European bullhead, for example, rely on smaller streams to raise their young and shelter from predators. If water levels fall, those habits could disconnect from the river, reduce oxygen levels and mean pollutants become more concentrated.

A sudden change in the river flow could mean species were unable to survive, she said.

"It's not a question of whether the Environment Agency is making the right or wrong decision because they don't necessarily have that choice, but what they should take into account is that these species are adapted to certain variations in river level.

"Will the Environment Agency be able to monitor that sufficiently?"

The agency said the effects of low levels were already being seen in parts of the river and its tributaries.

In south Shropshire, its river team has had to rescue fish from sections of the river.

Lawrence said that although the Severn was important for wildlife, it was also relied on by six million people for drinking water. Farmers also abstract water to irrigate crops.

"That balance for wildlife and people and the use of the river is really important and the drought order is going to help us provide that balance," he said.

articles.title: In 2016, a family donated its 42-acre Pennsylvania estate as a free public garden; after surviving an eminent-domain threat, Stoneleigh has now expanded by 10 acres to 52
articles.summary: US News: Two pieces of a historic Pennsylvania landscape were separated by a fence and a property line for more than a century. That division will soon be gone.
articles.body: Two pieces of a historic Pennsylvania landscape were separated by a fence and a property line for more than a century. That division will soon be gone. Stoneleigh: a natural garden, a former private estate is growing from 42 acres to 52 after acquiring most of the adjoining Oakwell property. The addition reconnects landscapes that were split nearly 100 years ago, providing a larger space for gardens, education and public enjoyment, states the Natural Lands website. The expansion is an unusual second chapter for Stoneleigh, which was converted to a free public garden in 2016 when the family that owned the estate gifted it to Natural Lands. Scroll down to read the details of the transformation.Bringing a historic landscape back togetherThe 10-acre addition is most of the 13-acre Oakwell property carved away from the original Stoneleigh estate in the 1920s and 1930s. The two properties are remarkably alike, yet they have been parted for generations. Visitors entering the northern garden path at Stoneleigh can glimpse soaring mature trees, historic architecture, and vestiges of previous garden designs that extend across the former property line. According to reports, the reunification will recapture a sense of the original scale of the landscape, while preserving the different histories that accrued on either side of the fence.A school project takes a turnThe expansion was not an easy journey by any means. The Lower Merion School District bought the 13-acre Oakwell property from three private homeowners in 2018. The district had intended to use the land for athletic fields related to plans for a nearby middle school. Plans were later changed because of public concern about the possible loss of the property's historic landscape and buildings. Five years after the purchase of Oakwell, the school district began to explore options with Natural Lands. Finally, the discussions resulted in a compromise which would save much of the property. Natural Lands will buy 10 acres to add to Stoneleigh and the remaining three acres will be passed to the Wyncote Foundation. This includes Oakwell Hall, which the foundation plans to restore and preserve.The future – A larger gardenThe new acreage will not be open to visitors right away. The added space will take several years of planning and restoration before it becomes part of Stoneleigh’s public experience. A new master plan offers a framework for integrating the two properties into a unified landscape. The expansion is expected to allow for more educational programming, enhanced visitor amenities, and new garden features while respecting the history of the area. The expanded garden will also contribute to Stoneleigh’s broader objective of highlighting the beauty and significance of the natural world and encouraging the cultivation of native plants.From threatened landscape to national treasureThe story of Oakwell’s preservation is testimony to the strength of community engagement in saving historic landscapes. Rather than becoming school athletic fields, the property will remain mostly a free public garden, and the historic mansion will have a future devoted to preservation. For Stoneleigh, the leap from 42 to 52 acres is more than an expansion. It means the re-establishment of a link that was lost generations ago. When the new acreage is prepared, visitors will find a landscape that is less like two properties side by side and more like what it was once: a single historic estate, now becoming a public garden for generations to come.Images Courtesy: Natural Lands and istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Northumberland foster carer praise Dolly Parton free book scheme
articles.summary: The singer's Imagination Library provides books for children up to age five across the world.
articles.body:
Foster carers have shared how Dolly Parton's free book scheme has helped children.

The country singer, who died on Tuesday, established her Imagination Library in 1995 in Tennessee to provide books from birth to age five, and it was then launched in the UK in 2007.

Barbara Hubbard, from Berwick, Northumberland, has been a carer for more than 10 years and said the scheme was "just amazing".

"Whenever I've had under-fives, I've had one of the Dolly Parton books arrive through my letterbox each month for that child," the 62-year-old told BBC Radio Newcastle.

"These books are for children to keep and we've had so many favourites.

"A lot of these children have speech problems and it's helped with their literacy.

"The little girl I've got now has special needs and yet she reads age-appropriately thanks to being in a home with lots of books."

Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has provided free books to millions of children in the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia and Republic of Ireland.

The initiative gives a book a month to children under five, with more than 300 million gifted worldwide.

In the UK alone, more than seven million books have been donated by the Imagination Library.

The principal of the Westmorland and Furness Virtual School in Cumbria, Sarah Roscoe-Campbell, has recently started distributing the books.

She told BBC Radio Cumbria: "Dolly's an international megastar who's from Tennessee in the USA, yet she has an impact on children and their reading here in Cumbria.

"We've had lots of positive feedback from foster carers around how they love to receive the books because it's actually about the connection and the relationship for the carer and the child."

Angela Morrison has also used the scheme during her five years as a foster carer.

She said: "Whenever I go out, I always pack the books in my bag.

"It's amazing how advanced some of the children have been with their speech when they've left us and I think a lot of that is down to reading the books."

In Northumberland, the county council operates the scheme and automatically sends books out to all eligible foster carers.

Social worker Leigh Finlay said the books had been "transformational" for some children in care.

"A lot of children who come into care haven't had that experience of sitting down and looking at a book," she said.

"In most arrangements, young children will move on from foster care, either to adoption or to return home with their parents, and their books will go with them."

articles.title: Nepal floods: From rescue to relief, India’s armed forces spring to action
articles.summary: News News: India's armed forces have, once again, stepped up beyond the country's own borders, and this is far from the first time. From responding to natural di.
articles.body: India's armed forces have, once again, stepped up beyond the country's own borders, and this is far from the first time. From responding to natural disasters to evacuating civilians caught in active war zones, the Army, Navy and Air Force have repeatedly rushed to the aid of citizens of other nations in distress, missions that have consistently showcased India's ability to mobilise and respond at short notice, often within hours of a crisis breaking out. This time too, just hours after the flash flood struck Nepal, the Indian Air Force, dispatched a C-130 transport aircraft with 10 tonnes of relief and medical material. The air force has stated that it would be sending more relief materials in the coming days through the larger C-17 as well.India sees itself as the first responder to any natural or man made calamity in the broader region centered around the Indian Ocean Region (IOR). India had first demonstrated its capability in this role during the 2004 Boxing Day tsunami that ravaged Indonesia as well as other parts of South East Asia. The ability to deploy men and material across the region in compressed timelines also demonstrates India's ability, if need be, to project power across the region to respond to any contingency. The air force and the army's Parachute Brigade had executed Operation Cactus, in which, responding to a developing coup in the Maldives, a force was sent to the island nation that effectively dismantled the coup event.During natural calamities too, the Indian armed forces have been quick to react and deploy assets to aid in the rescue and relief effort. The most recent instance came earlier this year with Operation Amistad in Venezuela, where two C-17 Globemaster aircraft carrying a full field hospital, 35 tonnes of relief supplies and a 41-member rescue team were dispatched to assist victims of a devastating earthquake, half the world away. Just months before that, in 2025, India launched Operation Sagar Bandhu for Sri Lanka after Cyclone Ditwah battered the island nation, helping restore critical communication links, evacuating over 2,500 people and delivering more than 1,000 tonnes of relief material. In the same year, following a powerful earthquake in Myanmar, the army set up a 60-bed field hospital under Operation Brahma. The navy and air force worked in tandem and ferried relief supplies to the affected region.2023 saw India mount three separate operations. Operation Dost saw Indian military aircraft and NDRF personnel rush to Turkey and Syria after a catastrophic earthquake flattened entire towns, delivering search-and-rescue teams and medical aid. The same year, Operation Kaveri evacuated thousands of Indian nationals from Sudan as fighting broke out between rival military factions in Khartoum, while Operation Karuna saw the armed forces deliver relief material to Myanmar in the aftermath of Cyclone Mocha.The year 2022 brought one of India's largest and most complex evacuation efforts in recent memory, Operation Ganga, which saw the Air Force and civilian carriers work around the clock to bring back over 20,000 Indian students and citizens stranded in Ukraine as Russia's invasion unfolded. A year earlier, as the Taliban swept back into power in Kabul, the Air Force carried out Operation Devi Shakti, airlifting Indian diplomats, officials and citizens out of Afghanistan under extremely tight security conditions.The Navy, too, has repeatedly proven its reach well beyond India's own coastline. In 2020, Operation Vanilla saw Indian naval ships rush relief material to Madagascar after a cyclone struck the island nation, even as the country grappled with the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. That same year, Operation Samudra Setu became one of the Navy's largest repatriation missions, bringing home thousands of stranded Indians by sea from Gulf countries and beyond. In 2017, Operation Insaniyat saw India send humanitarian aid to Bangladesh as it grappled with a massive influx of Rohingya refugees fleeing Myanmar.Earlier still, in 2016, Operation Sankat Mochan saw the Air Force airlift 156 Indian citizens to safety from Juba as fighting broke out in South Sudan. A year before that, in 2015, India carried out two of its most ambitious HADR missions yet, Operation Raahat, which evacuated over 4,700 Indians and nearly 2,000 foreign nationals from war-torn Yemen, and Operation Maitri, when India became the first country to respond to Nepal's devastating earthquake, rescuing thousands and setting up field hospitals within days. Even earlier, in 2014, Operation Neer saw the Navy rush emergency drinking water supplies to Male after a fire crippled the Maldivian capital's only water treatment plant.

articles.title: Humans stepped back from this UK dairy farm in 2023; three years later, wildlife returns as 27 more bird species appear and butterfly numbers more than double
articles.summary: UK News: A former dairy farm in the UK has undergone a striking transformation after humans stepped back and allowed natural processes to reshape the land. At .
articles.body: A former dairy farm in the UK has undergone a striking transformation after humans stepped back and allowed natural processes to reshape the land. At Heal Somerset, a 460-acre site in Somerset acquired by the rewilding charity Heal in December 2022, the first three years of nature recovery have brought a notable increase in wildlife. The number of recorded bird species has risen from 67 to 94, while butterfly species have increased from 11 to 24. The site has also recorded at least 15 bat species and 60 breeding bird species. The results, documented in Heal Somerset’s first State of Nature report, offer an early glimpse of what can happen when a landscape previously managed as farmland is given greater space for nature to recover.How a UK dairy farm became a rewilding projectHeal Somerset was acquired by the rewilding charity Heal Rewilding in December 2022, with nature recovery beginning in 2023. The 460-acre property had previously been operated as a dairy farm, but the organisation wanted to transform it into a landscape where natural processes could play a much greater role. Instead of continuing intensive farming, the project began moving the land towards rewilding, while retaining ecological monitoring and carrying out management where necessary. The aim was not simply to create a wildlife reserve but to allow habitats and ecological processes to develop over time. The Somerset project is also part of Heal Rewilding’s broader effort to demonstrate how degraded or intensively managed farmland can contribute to nature recovery in England.Bird species increased from 67 to 94The clearest early change has been recorded among birds. When monitoring began, 67 bird species were recorded at the site. Three years later, that figure had reached 94, meaning 27 additional species had been recorded. The increase does not necessarily mean that every one of those species established a permanent breeding population, but it demonstrates a substantial expansion in the range of birds using the landscape. The site now supports at least 60 breeding bird species, while the wider monitoring programme has also recorded species associated with a variety of habitats. Heal’s approach is to continue monitoring these changes so that future surveys can show whether the early gains develop into longer-term population recovery.Butterfly diversity more than doubledButterflies have shown an equally striking change. The number of butterfly species recorded at Heal Somerset increased from 11 to 24 during the three-year period, meaning the number of recorded species more than doubled. Such changes are significant because butterflies can respond relatively quickly to changes in vegetation and habitat structure, making them useful indicators of ecological conditions. The increase forms part of a wider picture of biodiversity recovery at the site, where monitoring has also documented bats and other small mammals. Rather than focusing on a single species, Heal’s State of Nature report is designed to examine changes across different groups of wildlife and establish a baseline against which future ecological recovery can be measured.What happens when nature is given more spaceThe project is based on the idea that rewilding does not always require humans to constantly manage every part of an ecosystem. Heal describes its approach as giving nature the space and time to lead the recovery process. That does not mean abandoning the land completely. The organisation continues ecological monitoring and undertakes necessary management, while also developing habitats and infrastructure that support wildlife and allow people to engage with the project. The approach is intended to rebuild wildlife populations, improve ecosystem resilience and reconnect communities with nature. Healthy ecosystems can also help regulate water flows, store carbon and improve soil structure, potentially making landscapes more resilient to climate extremes such as flooding and heatwaves.Next few years could matter even moreHeal Somerset’s three-year results are an early snapshot rather than proof that the entire ecosystem has already been restored. The charity itself plans to continue collecting ecological data and compare future results with the 2026 baseline. That long-term monitoring will be important because some changes may accelerate while others could take many years to become visible. The site also provides an opportunity to examine whether rewilding can deliver measurable biodiversity gains on land previously used for agriculture. For now, the jump from 67 to 94 recorded bird species and from 11 to 24 butterfly species provides a striking early indication that a landscape can change rapidly when intensive farming is replaced by a more nature-led approach. articles.title: 11,000-year-old sculpture of human seated on leopard found on a stone bench at Karahantepe in Türkiye reveals unique Neolithic art
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Archaeologists in southeastern Türkiye have unearthed an unusual 11,000-year-old stone sculpture showing a human figure seated on a leopard, offering .
articles.body: Archaeologists in southeastern Türkiye have unearthed an unusual 11,000-year-old stone sculpture showing a human figure seated on a leopard, offering a rare glimpse into the artistic world of one of the world's earliest settled communities. Archaeologists found the 70-centimetre-high figure at Karahantepe during the excavation period. The discovery is striking as the sculpture was found on a stone bench running along the wall of a circular structure about three metres across. According to T.C. Kültür ve Turizm Bakanlığı (Ministry of Culture and Tourism of the Republic of Turkey), Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy described the sculpture as a unique work with a style not previously seen at Karahantepe, saying the discovery could open the door to new questions about the earliest periods of human history. The discovery adds to growing evidence of the advanced artistic and architectural traditions that developed in the region during the Neolithic period, thousands of years before the emergence of cities and writing.11,000-year-old Karahantepe sculpture shows a human seated on a leopardAs reported, archaeologists found the 70-centimetre-high sculpture during the 2026 excavations at Karahantepe. The sculpture stands 70 centimetres high and depicts a person sitting on a leopard’s back. Archaeologists found the sculpture inside the structure, where it dates to around 11,000 years ago. The sculpture was found on a bench built along the wall of a circular structure about three metres in diameter. The ministry described the sculpture as unique, noting that its artistic style had not been seen before at Karahantepe. Its discovery within the structure also provides archaeologists with important context for studying the work and the setting in which it was placed.How Karahantepe offers a glimpse into the Neolithic periodKarahantepe belongs to a wider group of Neolithic settlements in southeastern Türkiye dating back to 11,000 years ago. During this period, communities were moving away from mobile hunter-gatherer lifestyles towards more settled ways of living. The archaeological record from the region includes large structures and sophisticated art, showing that people were developing complex social and ritual practices long before cities or writing appeared. A human figure seated on a leopard makes the sculpture particularly striking, although its original meaning cannot be established from the image alone.Where was the 11,000-year-old sculpture foundThe setting in which the sculpture was found adds important context to the discovery. It was found on a bench running along the wall of a circular structure rather than in soil. The structure measured about three metres in diameter. Its position within the structure provides important archaeological context for the finding. The relationship between the sculpture and the surrounding space may help researchers examine how it was positioned and what role it may have played. Its exact purpose, however, remains unclear.Why the human-and-leopard sculpture raises new questionsKarahantepe is helping archaeologists build a fuller picture of the Neolithic period and the people who lived in the region thousands of years ago. The site has produced substantial structures and a range of artworks, adding to the archaeological record of this early period. The newly discovered sculpture adds another unusual example, combining a human figure with a leopard. Its meaning remains uncertain, and the sculpture should not be taken as evidence that people rode or domesticated leopards.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Alix Earle has built her career by giving millions of followers an intimate look at her life, from beauty routines and relationships to family moments shared online. Now, the social media star is bringing that openness to Netflix with her upcoming reality series, “Earle Meets World.” One of the show's notable settings is her family’s New Jersey mansion, a property that has been part of the family’s life for more than a decade. According to Realtor.com, Earle’s family purchased the New Jersey mansion for $2.25 million in 2013, and the property is now estimated to be worth about $4.1 million. The home is also set to appear in the Netflix series, giving viewers a look inside the property where Earle’s father, stepmother and younger half-siblings live.A major real estate gainThe property was purchased by Alix’s father, Thomas “TJ” Earle, and her stepmother, Ashley Dupré, in 2013. Property records cited by Realtor.com show that the family paid $2.25 million for the home, considerably below its previous asking price of $3.35 million.More than a decade later, the estimated value has climbed to approximately $4.1 million. That represents an increase of around $1.85 million from the original purchase price. However, the $4.1 million figure is an estimated current value rather than the price from a recent sale. The change illustrates how the property has appreciated since the Earle family purchased it. The home has also been updated over time, with its interiors now looking different from the photographs that accompanied its original listing.The family’s New Jersey homeThe mansion is home to TJ and Ashley Earle and their younger children, while Alix and her sister, Ashtin, continue to spend time with the family when they are in New Jersey. As a result, the property is closely connected to the family relationships that will feature in the Netflix series. Rather than simply serving as an impressive luxury property, the house has become part of the family’s everyday life. It provides a familiar setting for family gatherings and conversations, making it a natural location for a reality show focused heavily on the dynamics between Earle family members.Alix’s relationship with her family has already been visible through her social media content. However, the Netflix series promises to show those relationships on a much larger scale and with cameras capturing interactions beyond the short videos she typically produces herself.A family at the centre“Earle Meets World” brings together several members of Alix’s family, including her father, stepmother, mother Alisa, sister Ashtin and younger half-siblings. Their relationships are expected to form an important part of the program. The trailer offers glimpses of emotional and tense conversations, particularly surrounding the complicated relationship between Alix’s mother and stepmother. The show also follows aspects of Alix’s personal life and her experiences following her breakup with NFL player Braxton Berrios.That makes the New Jersey mansion more than just a backdrop. It is one of the places where the family’s complicated relationships can unfold naturally, giving viewers a setting they can return to throughout the series.From TikTok to NetflixEarle first became widely known through TikTok, where her candid “get ready with me” videos helped turn her into a major social media personality. Her popularity grew because of the informal way she discussed beauty, relationships, parties and everyday experiences with her followers.Moving to Netflix marks a significant expansion of that format. On social media, Earle has considerable control over what she records and publishes. A television production, however, gives viewers access to interactions captured by a professional production team. This difference could make the series particularly interesting for people who already follow Earle online. Instead of seeing carefully selected snippets of her life, audiences will be able to watch longer conversations and family interactions within a structured reality-TV format.The mansion gets a new roleThe New Jersey property has therefore taken on a new role. For more than a decade, it has been the Earle family home and a place familiar to those who follow Alix online. Now, it is becoming part of the visual identity of her first major Netflix series.The property's estimated rise from $2.25 million to $4.1 million also adds a real estate angle to the story. While its financial appreciation is notable, the home’s importance to the family goes beyond its price tag. As “Earle Meets World” brings Alix’s family life to a wider audience, viewers will see the mansion not simply as a multimillion-dollar New Jersey property, but as a setting for the relationships, disagreements and everyday moments that shape the Earle family.A familiar setting on screenThe mansion’s appearance in the series creates a connection between the Alix Earle audiences know from social media and the family life that exists away from her online platforms. Its rooms and shared spaces will provide a familiar backdrop as the show explores her career, relationships and family dynamics.With the series scheduled to premiere on Netflix on September 4, 2026, the longtime family home is about to become recognisable to an even larger audience. articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away
articles.summary: One woman says her father, mother, sister and sister's children were carried away before her eyes.
articles.body:
Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.

More than 175 people have died and 800 others are missing after floods wiped out entire villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, with a force so powerful seismologists initially identified it as an earthquake.

Rescuers trudged through thick mud and debris on Thursday as Nepalese authorities rushed to bring aid and relief supplies to the affected areas.

"My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes," Kalpana Malla from Nepal's Nuwakot district told the BBC.

Malla said her father, mother, sister and sister's children were all claimed by the disaster.

"They could not escape the flood; there was no chance at all," she said. "This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived but couldn't explain how."

Her son, Sugam Malla, said he saved his mother by pulling her hand.

He said he had given his phone to his sister so she could keep in touch, but the mobile was no longer reachable.

Another woman, Goma Pandit, said she had lost her buffaloes and all her other cattle.

"My farmland is also swept away. Ten sacks of mustard seeds, tons of corn and rice paddy are all gone. Nothing is left."

At Kathmandu's TU Teaching Hospital, families of those missing in the floods wait anxiously for updates.

Holding up her phone, Ram Khumari Shrestha says: "This is my husband. He was off to Rasuwa as a part of his driving job. He was in contact with me until 8 pm yesterday.

"But I couldn't call him this morning. The phone was switched off," she told the BBC.

Mani Shrestha Bishwa was also camped out at the hospital on Wednesday night, hoping to hear from his younger brother, cousin, uncle and friend.

"I last contacted them at 8:30 in the morning," he said.

Trekking guide Sonam Dorjee missed the flood in his home village of Rasiwa Syafru by about an hour. He had left at 08:00 local time.

As he was driving to Kathmandu, Dorjee told the BBC he had heard the sound of floods gushing into their village.

"It [sounded] like an earthquake," he said. "My house has collapsed... I have seen a photo."

Dorjee said his sister, Dechen Tamang, was missing, along with her husband and several other family members.

He described the flood as "sudden and devastating".

"Many survivors are now left without homes and they need emergency rescue and evacuation, as well as food, temporary accommodation and medical support."

He is praying his sister is found alive. "There is a 10% chance, we hope," he said.

articles.title: Ben Shapiro’s anti-Muslim film is nothing new
articles.summary: Shapiro’s film recycles decades-old anti-Muslim tropes to portray critics of Israel’s genocide in Gaza as extremists.
articles.body:
Ben Shapiro, prominent pro-Israel blogger and co-founder of the far-right news site The Daily Wire, claims Hollywood has spent the last three decades refusing to tell the story of “the threat of radical Islam”.

As an American Muslim woman, an avid movie-goer, and a human with eyes, I must say that statement’s pretty delusional – even for a known bigot like Shapiro, who once declared, “Arabs like to bomb crap and live in open sewage.”

While announcing the trailer for his Islamophobic new film, Run Hide Fight: Infidels, Shapiro posted on X that “the threat of radical Islam is real” and that Hollywood has “refused to tell that story for three decades”. He described his film as the “biggest, most audacious, funniest and most kickass film” The Daily Wire has ever released.

I’m not sure what’s supposed to be audacious about making Muslims the bad guys; Hollywood has been doing that since before I was born.

In 2003, American writer and educator Jack Shaheen published Reel Bad Arabs based on his review of more than 900 films featuring Arab characters. He found that Hollywood routinely blurred Arab and Muslim identities and overwhelmingly portrayed them as violent, barbaric, greedy, sexually threatening, or otherwise dangerous.

And you don’t have to take Shaheen’s word for it. Just take a look at a few of the movies.

In True Lies (1994), Arab terrorists plot to detonate a nuclear weapon in the United States. Executive Decision (1996) features Muslim terrorists hijacking a plane and associates Islamic prayer and Quranic imagery with terrorism. The Siege (1998) envisions terrorist attacks in New York that lead to the arrests of Arab Americans. Rules of Engagement (2000) portrays US Marines killing Yemeni civilians, then proceeds to justify it.

I distinctly remember the horrific surge in anti-Muslim threats and comments on social media when American Sniper, a film that dehumanises and demonises the Iraqi people, came out in 2015.

Television shows didn’t exactly take a different approach. Shows such as 24 and Homeland built major storylines around Muslim terrorists, sleeper cells, and the possibility that Muslim communities were sheltering extremists.

At times, Hollywood did give us slightly improved versions of the same story: The “good” Arab or Muslim character who helps the Americans fight the “bad” Muslims. For example, in the 2007 action thriller The Kingdom, a Saudi police officer partners with American agents to help them investigate and fight off terrorists. While it is a little better than every Arab or Muslim character being a terrorist, it still leaves us with limited options: We are either the bad guys or the exception who sees the error in our people’s barbaric ways.

In more recent years, however, Muslims have been seeing more complex and nuanced representations of ourselves in shows and films such as Ramy, Mo, Ms Marvel, and the yet-unreleased Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother. While these dramatic fictional portrayals do not always embody how Muslims strive to live their faith and ideals in everyday life, they have helped expand public understanding of the diversity of Muslim experiences.

But that doesn’t change basic history or undo the harm that’s already been done by decades of Hollywood using “Muslim” and “Arab” as shorthand for “terrorist” and “extremist”. This portrayal of Muslims and Arabs as threats that need to be neutralised has real consequences. In May this year, anti-Muslim extremists filmed themselves violently attacking the Islamic Center of San Diego, fatally shooting three men who sacrificed their lives to stop the attackers from making their way to young children in the Islamic school on the mosque’s premises.

However, I will give Shapiro some credit. He did try to put a modern spin on those tired, old anti-Muslim tropes.

According to the film’s trailer, the story centres on a college campus taken over by “radical Islamic terrorists” who seize a Gaza solidarity encampment, establish what the movie calls a “makeshift caliphate”, impose “Sharia law”, and execute “infidels”.

It also juxtaposes ISIL (ISIS) imagery and footage from 9/11 with footage of the 2024 protests on college campuses, taking a real political movement – students protesting Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza – and putting it in the same fictional frame as extremist violence.

Since October 7, Palestinians, Muslims, and their allies have increasingly been treated by the US political establishment as security threats. Palestinian solidarity has routinely been treated as suspect. College protesters have been accused of being sympathetic to terrorists. American Muslims have been accused of being anti-Semitic for criticising a foreign government that is actively committing genocide.

Now, here comes a movie that turns an anti-genocide campus encampment into the starting point for an “Islamist” takeover of America. It is an old far-right conspiracy theory, repackaged as a new film.

We also can’t ignore its questionable timing.

The film’s promotion comes at a time when anti-Muslim hate, spurred in part by the Israeli government’s attempt to distract people from the bad PR of committing genocide, is already at an all-time high; as we head into another election season, with voters increasingly turning against AIPAC-funded candidates who refuse to condemn or take action against Israel’s genocide in Gaza; and as The Daily Wire and Shapiro himself no longer hold the same level of influence they once had. And what better way to stay relevant than to take a popular, if not played-out, subject, update it, and tell everyone you’re brave enough to tell a new story that Hollywood was too afraid to tell?

Except he’s not. He’s just recycling one that Hollywood has been telling for decades and attaching it to the political argument he wants to make today.

For those of us who have been negatively impacted by this blatantly inaccurate portrayal of Muslims for our whole lives, it’s definitely not new or brave.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: In 2019, A Tasmanian couple used a $1.6m bequest to buy Prosser River Reserve near Orford; years later, it held 11 at-risk species and 14 vegetation communities
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Tasmanian couple's generous $1.6 million bequest led to the purchase of Prosser River Reserve, a sanctuary for 11 threatened species and 14 unique vegetation communities, highlighting the impact of targeted conservation efforts.
articles.body: In 2019, a Tasmanian couple used a 1.6 million family bequest to help buy more than 1,500 hectares of bushland near Orford on the state's east coast. The land, now known as Prosser River Reserve, has since been confirmed to hold 11 threatened plant and animal species and 14 distinct vegetation communities, making it a significant private reserve in the state.The purchase was funded by the estate of David McGregor, whose family had a long-standing connection to conservation work in Tasmania. His son Bruce and daughter-in-law Ann used the bequest to enable the Tasmanian Land Conservancy to acquire the property outright, rather than simply donating funds toward an existing project. According to the Tasmanian Land Conservancy reserve page, the family had a preferred site in mind from the outset and worked closely with the conservancy to make sure the purchase matched David's wishes for the money. The property sits just outside Buckland, where the Prosser and Back Rivers cut through a valley of grassy woodland near Tasmania's east coast. That combination of varied terrain and underlying geology was associated with more ecological diversity than a typical block of similar size, a point the conservancy highlighted when the purchase was first made public.Where Old Forest Still StandsSome sections of the property had been selectively logged over the decades, but large areas were left largely untouched. Surveys later found at least 500 hectares of old-growth and undisturbed forest still standing across the reserve, providing shelter and nesting habitat that younger, previously cleared woodland simply cannot match. That older forest, combined with the freshwater systems running through the valley, gave ecologists far more to work with than they initially expected from a property that had spent part of its history under commercial use.Six of the vegetation communities eventually mapped on the reserve are listed as threatened under Tasmanian law, and one, black gum woodland, carries a critically endangered listing under federal legislation as well. That level of protection is notable for a single privately acquired property, and it reflects the ecological value that remained on land that was little known outside the local area.A home for devils, quolls and swift parrots The reserve is home to many of Tasmania's best-known threatened species. Tasmanian devils, eastern quolls, spotted-tailed quolls and eastern barred bandicoots all use the property, alongside masked owls, grey goshawks and white-bellied sea eagles that nest in the older forest sections. The swift parrot, one of Australia's most critically endangered birds, also passes through the area during its migratory cycle. Local legal commentary published by the Law Society of Tasmania noted that the species now benefit from formal conservation protection on land that might otherwise have remained in private hands.The reserve also carries deep cultural significance that predates its conservation history by centuries. The Payintaymirimina band of the Oyster Bay tribe once used a route along the Prosser River now known as the old convict road, later repurposed and paved with bluestone bricks during the colonial period. That layered history, spanning Aboriginal land use, convict labour and now private conservation can add another dimension to a property that was purchased primarily for its ecological value.Bruce McGregor's later recognition with an Order of Australia honour cited his role in permanently protecting Prosser River Reserve as one of the defining achievements of a lifetime spent supporting conservation work. For a family that described itself as not especially wealthy but deeply committed to nature, the reserve shows how a well-directed bequest can deliver significant ecological benefits.Unlike broader donations, a bequest tied to a specific piece of land ensures the money goes to that property and gives donors a lasting connection to the outcome. Weeding days and monitoring visits still bring together conservancy staff and members of the McGregor family. They remain involved with the property years after the original purchase closed, keeping the reserve's story visible whenever the subject of legacy giving comes up among prospective donors weighing how best to direct their own estates.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: People deserve to feel safe in their own homes, says Redcar and Cleveland council leader
articles.summary: Teesside MPs and a council leader say communities need to feel safe after the incidents over the past week.
articles.body:
People living in a town where nine people have been killed in a crash and fire in the past week deserve to "feel safe in their own homes", a council leader has said.

Redcar and Cleveland Borough Council leader Alec Brown's comments come after seven people, including two police officers, died in a car crash at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on Saturday and a 34-year-old woman and seven-year-old girl died in a house fire in Grangetown on Wednesday.

Brown told Radio 4's Today programme he had called an "urgent meeting" on Friday among councillors, police and social housing providers.

Teesside MPs also called for the government to provide more support for police and firefighters in the area.

Police have made several arrests in connection with the recent deaths.

Brown said he understood people from parts of Middlesbrough and Redcar might feel "left behind".

"I'm from an estate, from the same ilk," he said.

"You live around people that may be suffering poverty or other social issues, it can be that uniform sort of consciousness that 'we're left behind'.

"But I can assure the people of Grangetown and South Bank – they're as important to me as a people from any other state in the borough and we're working tirelessly to ensure that they do feel safe in their own houses."

Labour MPs Anna Turley, Luke Myer, Andy McDonald, Jonathan Brash and Chris McDonald said in a joint statement their communities deserved to "feel safe".

They said they welcomed the help of other police forces during the past week but called for more long-term support for officers in the area.

They said local residents had expressed "safety concerns" for "far too long".

Myer said current national funding formulas for the police and fire service did not take into account the "seriousness" of the crime people in Teesside faced.

"We essentially have a metropolitan style of crime and also risk of fire but with a sort of rural-style funding," he said.

"This is why we need to see a real overhaul of the funding formula."

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died on Saturday when a Volkswagen Passat, going the wrong way on the A66 at South Bank hit their vehicle.

The five young men in the Volkswagen also died.

Police said 17 people, aged between 18 and 61, had been arrested across Teesside as part of an ongoing investigation into the lead-up to the crash.

They have been held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

On Wednesday Natalie McDonald, 34, died along with her seven-year-old niece, Valentina Foster, in the fire in Grangetown.

Cleveland Police said the blaze had also left a 48-year-old woman in a critical condition in hospital alongside another three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and were in police custody, the force said.

It said it was "keeping an open mind" about the fire and said it could not "rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

articles.title: In 2007, Texas sank the retired 473-foot Texas Clipper off South Padre Island; it now brings in over $1 million from anglers and up to $2 million from divers
articles.summary: US News: Discover how the Texas Clipper, sunk in 2007 off South Padre Island, became a lucrative artificial reef, generating millions for local economy and boosting marine biodiversity.
articles.body: In November 2007, Texas transformed the retired 473-foot USTS Texas Clipper from a former passenger liner and maritime training ship into an artificial reef in the Gulf of Mexico. The vessel was deployed about 17 miles off South Padre Island, where its steel hull and multiple decks provided hard surfaces for marine organisms and shelter for fish after it was sunk. Nearly two decades later, the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) says that the Texas Clipper reef generatesmore than $1 million from anglers and approximately $1.4 million to $2 million from divers.Transformation from a wartime transport to a Texas training shipThe vessel’s history began long before it reached the Gulf seafloor. Built by Bethlehem Steel in Maryland, it was commissioned by the US Navy in December 1944 as USS Queens (APA-103). During the Second World War, the ship carried troops and supplies in the Pacific and transported wounded Marines from combat areas. Following the war, the vessel was converted for civilian passenger service and renamed SS Ecambion, operating on Mediterranean routes.The ship’s next major chapter began in 1965, when it became the USTS Texas Clipper, a training vessel used by Texas A&M University at Galveston. Until 1996, it remained in that role, giving maritime students and cadets practical experience at sea. TPWD describes the ship’s eventual reefing as its fourth and permanent life, after its military, passenger and training careers.When the ageing training vessel was no longer required, the Texas officials opted for an alternative instead of simply scrapping it. Immediately following its 1996 retirement, the Texas Artificial Reef Program pursued the vessel as a potential offshore reef; however, converting a large ship into a marine habitat required extensive preparation. According to TPWD, the vessel was transferred to the state on 4 October 2006, after nearly a decade of negotiations with the US Maritime Administration.Subsequently, the ship was towed from the reserve fleet in Beaumont to a shipyard in Brownsville, where it underwent extensive environmental preparation. The aim was to ensure that the structure would be suitable for deliberate placement in the marine environment.Preparing a 473-foot ship for the seafloorBefore deployment, crews removed materials that could contaminate the Gulf. TPWD says the preparation included about 7,000 gallons of hydrocarbons, 1,680 cubic yards of asbestos, 393,270 pounds of PCB-containing materials, 1,410 cubic yards of debris and 330,450 gallons of wastewater. Additionally, workers altered the ship’s structure. Large openings were cut into the hulls so that seawater could circulate through the vessel and marine organisms and fish could use its interior spaces. Following these heavy shipyard modifications, a massive final cleanup sweep was executed to purge 1,410 cubic yards of loose operational and industrial debris from the ship prior to its tow.In November 2007, the Texas Clipper was deployed as an artificial reef, coming to rest approximately 17 miles off South Padre Island. Instead of disappearing into the Gulf as scrap, the vessel became a permanent hard structure in an offshore environment where natural reef habitat was comparatively limited.The ship became an economic and ecological assetOnce established underwater, the Texas Clipper became part of the marine environment rather than just an inert object on the seafloor. Sponges, corals, barnacles, and other marine organisms colonised the artificial-reef structures, while diverse fish populations utilised the shelter created by the ship’s hull and superstructure. Biological monitoring at the site has documented a thriving ecosystem, cementing the vessel's status as one of the state's most ecologically successful deep-water habitats.The state agency has reported that the sunken vessel now generates more than $1 million for the local economy from anglers and approximately $1.4 million to $2 million from divers. These figures reflect estimated recreational economic activity associated with the site, instead of the money earned directly by the ship or reef.Furthermore, the Clipper has an unusual distinction within Texas’ artificial-reef programme. The agency identifies the vessel as the largest ship intentionally sunk under this programme. Its size gives marine organisms an unusually extensive and complex structure to colonise, while its location makes it accessible to recreational visitors travelling from the South Padre Island region.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Birmingham weather warning as 'significant flooding' leads to fire service callouts
articles.summary: Heavy rain creates problems for residents, with flood alerts in place on Thursday across the region.
articles.body:
Flooding has hit the West Midlands after heavy rain.

The Environment Agency (EA) issued a flood warning for Birmingham on Wednesday night, with fire crews called to "significant flooding" in Perry Barr around Curbar Road, Thornbridge Avenue and Haddon Road, telling people to avoid the area.

In south Staffordshire there was a lower-level flood alert, with parts of Chasetown affected. The alert remains in place.

A yellow thunderstorm warning is also in place for England until 22:00 BST on Thursday, with Birmingham seeing heavy downpours just before 08:00 although the flood warning is now removed. Another, however, has been introduced for Bromsgrove, Worcestershire.

It was issued for the Spadesbourne Brook area, with the EA saying rising river levels were expected to cause flooding of roads and properties including the Midland Waterlife Centre.

Other parts of the West Midlands were subject to fresh flood alerts on Thursday, with areas of the Black Country, Warwickshire and Shropshire said to be at potential risk.

Despite scaling down its warning for Birmingham, the EA said standing water and debris could persist in the city on Thursday.

Chasetown resident Sue Woodhouse said flooding on Saint Annes Close on Wednesday evening was "the worst we've seen it in the last seven years of living here".

"It was awful, absolutely awful, never seen rain like it - flooding everywhere," she said. "It came right to the grass, right up above the curbs and flooded the whole cul de sac really."

She said heavy rain had returned on Thursday morning.

"I reckon we're going to get flooded yet again," she said. "I don't think it'll come in the house but it might come up the garden."

She added that she was concerned that the elderly residents of the cul-de-sac, who were in bed when the flood hit last night, would not be able to leave their homes.

She said the water there was "really deep".

Remaining flood alerts in the wider West Midlands on Thursday morning included the River Blythe in Warwickshire and the River Stour and Smestow Brook in the Black Country and south Staffordshire.

The River Cole and Rea were also subject to alerts, although the EA was not able to offer detail as to specific risk locations.

The Upper Tame at Sandwell Valley also featured on the list.

Flooding may affect low lying land and roads adjacent to the River Salwarpe from Catshill to Hawford in Worcestershire, according to the EA.

Other areas that may be at risk in the county include Stoke Prior, Elmley Lovett, Droitwich Spa and Ombersley.

In Shropshire, Stoke Heath was added to the list.

articles.title: Muff: Concerns over impact of quad bikes on natural wildlife
articles.summary: A resident of Carnamoyle says quad bike riders in Lisnagra Woods have been impacting local wildlife.
articles.body:
Concerns have been raised over the impact of quad bike riders on wildlife in a woodland area near Muff, County Donegal in the Republic of Ireland.

Margaret Peoples, who is from Carnamoyle, said people riding quad bikes in Lisnagra Woods have been visiting the area throughout the summer.

Peoples said the quad bikes are causing significant damage to the woodland, making the area difficult for families and dog walkers to use, while also cutting up the forest floor, which is impacting plants and wildlife.

She said the noise and damage caused by the heavy vehicles are particularly concerning for a colony of red squirrels, at a time when they are gathering and storing food ahead of winter.

"These quads have been cutting the place up every weekend," Peoples told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Thursday.

"It's been happening all summer, and it's making the place nearly unusable for people coming with their kids, or for a walk with the dog or whatever, because it's very badly cut up and mucky at the minute.

"Plus, it's also doing a lot of damage to the forest floor, which is bad for the survival of the woods, for the food chain in the woods, for the seeds and the birds.

"It's not the place for quads. It really isn't."

"The damage that they're doing to the forest floor and the undergrowth, where the small mammals – your squirrels, your rabbits, your pine martens – are at this time of year gathering up for the winter, they're wrecking that.

"And the noise disturbance is clearly going to be an issue for any bird life. Even now, there's not as much birdsong in the morning or afternoon as there would have been before all this started."

"We have a colony of red squirrels here who are having to deal with all this disturbance, you know, these things need peace and quiet to thrive.

"It's their home. We're only visitors there, and we need to respect that if they're going to survive and thrive."

Peoples urged the quad bike riders to take their activities to an area that is more appropriate.

Sinn Féin councillor Terry Crossan said he has raised concerns over the quad bikes with Coillte Ireland, the forestry company responsible for managing 440,000 hectares of primarily forested land across the Republic of Ireland and An Garda Síochána (the Irish police service).

Crossan said there were potential dangers to families walking in the woods while vehicles are travelling at high speeds.

"This has been going on for quite some time and is happening on a regular basis.

"This activity in the Lisnagra area is causing severe loss of habitat and is having a detrimental impact on wildlife, especially the red squirrels and pine martens.

"Any noise pollution or damage to habitat or vegetation all has a very serious impact, with a lot of areas in the wood being turned into an absolute quagmire.

"I have contacted Coillte and Gardaí over these repeated incidents of quad bikes being ridden in the woodland, and hopefully we will see some action in the immediate future."

articles.title: Tarr's ice cream shop in Bristol closes after 106 years
articles.summary: The Tarr family say they are "devastated" to announce they will have to close due to rising costs.
articles.body:
Staff at a much-loved family-run ice cream business say they are "devastated" after announcing it is closing its doors after 106 years of business due to rising costs.

Tarr's Ice Cream first opened in the Brislington area of Bristol in the 1920s and fast became a place where local families would head to get a treat. It was also named Bristol's Family Business of the Year in 2018.

But after weathering through the lockdowns of Covid-19 and struggling with the continuing rising costs of operating, the family said things were "extremely difficult" to sustain.

Bradley Tarr, a fourth generation member of the family, said: "It is a sad time... but it's had to happen unfortunately."

The 41-year-old said many factors including Brexit, the pandemic and the rising cost of living prompted by ongoing conflict around the world had pushed up the prices associated with running the business.

He added that he found an old annual electric bill from 2012 for £14,000, compared to last year's bill of £78,000.

Although Bradley said it was a sad time, he said the situation was "easier" for him to come to terms with as he had seen the business "struggle more" compared to his older relatives.

"I feel more sorry for the people who have spent their whole lives doing it - my grandad, my great auntie Vera, my auntie Deana who's still working in the business, my mum - who's worked there ever since I can remember - my sister who still works there part-time... it's very sad, but I know it's the right time," he said.

He added that the family felt "a cocktail of emotions" with a mixture of pride and sadness, but they would remember the good times.

In a post on social media which gained thousands of responses from customers past and present, the family shared a "heartfelt thank you".

"We have had to make this upsetting and difficult decision to pull the shutters down for the very last time," they said.

"Life in this world has become extremely difficult for small family-run businesses to stay open.

"We tried our best to keep our dream and love for ice cream alive as long as we could.

"At the end of an era comes with great sadness, our final chapter is closing."

The family said they planned to keep the shop open to sell remaining stock before closing the doors for good after November.

articles.title: Influencer shot dead in Mexico while livestreaming: Suspect arrested in cartel-hit Sinaloa
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Mexico has arrested a man suspected of shooting dead influencer Cesar Gastelum during a livestream earlier this month, authorities said Wednesday, as .
articles.body: Mexico has arrested a man suspected of shooting dead influencer Cesar Gastelum during a livestream earlier this month, authorities said Wednesday, as investigators linked the killing to his social media posts.Gastelum was attacked on August 4 while livestreaming in Culiacan, the capital of Sinaloa state, a region caught in a violent conflict between rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel.Gastelum, who had more than 500,000 followers on TikTok, was dressed as a food delivery worker and taking part in a social media challenge with two friends when a motorcycle stopped beside him. One of the two riders then shot him in the head.Mexico's Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said the suspected gunman was located in Puebla state in central Mexico.Police officers came under attack from three armed individuals during the arrest operation, Harfuch said on X. Officers killed one of the attackers and arrested the alleged killer of Gastelum along with another person.A preliminary investigation found that the influencer's killing was linked to his social media posts "alluding to a faction of a criminal group," Mexico's security secretariat said.The killing comes amid a violent conflict between the two main factions of the Sinaloa Cartel and allied armed groups in Sinaloa. The fighting has left thousands of people dead or missing as President Claudia Sheinbaum's government seeks to curb organised crime and violence.The Sinaloa Cartel was founded by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman, who is serving a prison sentence in the United States.Culiacan is also regarded as a centre of Mexico's "narco-culture", where the lives of drug traffickers are celebrated on social media and in popular culture. Mexican media have reported that some social media influencers have links to rival criminal groups, making them targets of intimidation and retaliation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Michael Sheen hopes reaction to toxic waste documentary spurs action
articles.summary: Dozens of people contacted BBC Wales following coverage of Sheen's investigation into chemical giant Monsanto.
articles.body:
Michael Sheen has welcomed the reaction to his documentary investigating Wales' toxic waste legacy, saying he hopes it pushes the relevant authorities to "find a solution".

Dozens of people contacted BBC Wales following coverage of Sheen's investigation into chemical giant Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).

One of them was a former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping to seal toxic waste underground and said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.

Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond to either Sheen and his team or the BBC when asked to comment.

Asked about the response to the documentary, Sheen said he wanted "to see something actually happen".

"So getting a response was a really important part of it, and hoping that response would push the people who are in positions to get on with it," he said.

Sheen said he had received "extraordinary messages" from people who wanted to tell their stories and how they had been affected.

"There's a lot of stuff for us to follow up," he said.

Sheen said he hoped "people in the more official areas" would respond as well and "work with us on it".

"We want to find a solution rather than something that keeps putting people in a position where they have to put breaks on because they can't afford to get involved in this, so we really want to find a solution to this."

Much of the documentary focuses on researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan, who tried to raise the alarm about 14 sites - 12 of which were in Wales - but died before his warnings were heeded.

"What he told me made my blood run cold," said Sheen, who spoke to Gowan months before he died.

Gowan, a former farming consultant, alleged that chemical giant Monsanto had dumped "huge amounts of industrial chemicals all around Wales".

Following coverage of the documentary, people contacted BBC Wales to speak about their experience, including Stephen Constance, 61, who worked at Monsanto's Newport factory in the 1990s.

He described working for the company as "absolutely dreadful".

Natural Resources Wales previously said "the legacy of historic industrial activity" in the UK and globally was an issue, most of which "took place before modern environmental regulations were in place", the "records can be limited and the nature of waste is not always fully known".

The Welsh government previously said that "addressing contaminated land" was a key priority.
